1. 💰 BANKING, MONETARY POLICY & FINANCIAL REGULATION

BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 1

RBI Relaxes Capital Requirements for Bank Loans under ECLGS 5.0 (Split Risk-Weight Structure)

  • Regulatory Framework & Mandate: Reserve Bank of India issued an amendment to the Master Direction – RBI (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025, significantly easing capital requirements for bank loans backed by the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS 5.0).
  • Split Risk-Weight Mechanism: • 75% of the Guaranteed Portion: Attracts a 0% risk weight, meaning banks are completely exempt from setting aside regulatory capital against this portion of the exposure. • Remaining 25% Exposure: Attracts a concessional 20% risk weight (drastically reduced from standard unrated exposure weights).
  • Settlement Condition for 0% Weight: • Banks can avail of the 0% risk weight benefit only if the guarantee claim is settled within 30 days from the date of invocation. • If the 30-day settlement requirement is breached, the benefit of the 0% risk weight is revoked, and standard capital charges apply.
  • Strategic Intent: Designed to release trapped bank capital, incentivize fresh liquidity flow to distressed and contact-intensive businesses, and align sovereign-backed portfolio risk with Basel III Pillar 1 norms.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Risk-Weight Split: 0% on 75% of guaranteed portion vs 20% on remaining 25% (a classic matching/statement MCQ).
  • Time Boundary for Settlement: Must be settled within 30 days of claim invocation to retain 0% risk weight.
  • Policy Anchor: Governed under the RBI (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions.
DISPATCH № 2

Launch of ARIFAC: National Industry Platform for AML/CFT Compliance with FIU-IND Oversight

  • Genesis & Institutional Architecture: India's financial sector formally launched the Alliance of Reporting Entities in AML/CFT (ARIFAC) as a premier national industry-led coordination platform to bolster Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (CFT) frameworks.
  • Administrative Secretariat: Jointly managed and operated by the Payments Council of India (PCI) and the Fintech Convergence Council (FCC).
  • Official Regulatory Observer: The Financial Intelligence Unit – India (FIU-IND) participates in ARIFAC in an official observer role, offering high-level guidance, regulatory alignment, and supervisory coordination.
  • Universal Membership Base: Encompasses all reporting entities regulated under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA): • Commercial Banks and Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs). • Payment System Operators (PSOs) and Payment Aggregators (PAs). • Securities market intermediaries, Mutual Funds, and Depository Participants. • Insurance companies and Virtual Digital Asset (VDA) service providers.
  • Operational Focus: Standardizing suspicious transaction reporting (STR) formats, conducting joint capacity-building certifications, and creating early-warning networks to intercept financial mule rings.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Joint Secretariat: Payments Council of India (PCI) + Fintech Convergence Council (FCC) (NOT IBA alone).
  • Observer Agency: FIU-IND (Financial Intelligence Unit – India).
  • Legislative Anchor: Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002.
POLICY & STRATEGIC ACCORDS № 3

Credit Guarantee Scheme for Microfinance Institutions 2.0 (CGSMFI-2.0): Expansion to ₹20,000 Crore Pool

  • Framework Evolution: Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services – DFS) and NCGTC operationalized CGSMFI-2.0, transitioning from emergency COVID-era relief (launched 28 June 2021) into a permanent, risk-based, tier-structured credit enhancement framework.
  • Pool Size & Validity: • Total guarantee pool expanded to ₹20,000 crore. • Extended validity up to 31 August 2026 (or until the ₹20,000 Cr guarantees are fully exhausted).
  • NCGTC Institutional Profile: • Implemented by National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company Limited (NCGTC), set up under DFS, Ministry of Finance (established in Union Budget 2013-14; incorporated 28 March 2014 under Companies Act 1956; paid-up capital ₹10 crore; Headquartered in Mumbai).
  • Three-Tier MFI Classification & Loan Limits: • Small-size MFIs (AUM < ₹500 crore): Max loan capacity capped at 20% of AUM, subject to a maximum of ₹100 crore; NCGTC guarantee cover of 80%; mandatory bank allocation of minimum 5% of bank's scheme pool. • Medium-size MFIs (AUM ₹500 crore to < ₹2,000 crore): Max loan capacity capped at 20% of AUM, subject to a maximum of ₹200 crore; NCGTC guarantee cover of 75%; mandatory bank allocation of minimum 10% of bank's scheme pool. • Large-size MFIs (AUM ≥ ₹2,000 crore): Max loan capacity enhanced upward from ₹300 crore to ₹1,000 crore (subject to 20% of AUM); NCGTC guarantee cover of 70%; eligible for remaining available pool.
  • Interest Rate & On-Lending Structure: • Lending Rate to MFIs (MLIs to MFIs): Capped at EBLR or MCLR + 2.0% per annum. • On-Lending Rate to Borrowers: Capped at 1.0% below the MFI's average lending rate of the preceding six months.
  • Guarantee Fee & Utilization: • Guarantee fee fixed at 0.50% per annum on the sanctioned amount in the 1st year, and on outstanding balance from Year 2 onwards. • Minimum 80% of funds must be deployed for fresh microfinance loan assets within 4 months.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Large MFI Max Loan Ceiling: Enhanced from ₹300 Cr to ₹1,000 crore (capped at 20% of AUM).
  • Tier-wise Guarantee Cover: Small = 80%, Medium = 75%, Large = 70%.
  • Interest Spread Cap: Lending to MFIs capped at EBLR/MCLR + 2%; on-lending capped at 1% below average rate.
  • NCGTC Foundation: Incorporated 28 March 2014; initial paid-up capital ₹10 crore.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 4

RBI Master Directions on Bank Lending to REITs & InvITs (49% Aggregate Exposure Cap)

  • Policy Harmonization: RBI released the Master Directions on Bank Lending to Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs), permitting scheduled commercial banks to lend directly to business trusts under strict prudential boundaries.
  • Eligibility & Asset Composition Norms: • Banks can lend only to SEBI-registered and publicly listed REITs and InvITs. • Operational Asset Threshold: At least 80% of the underlying assets of the borrowing REIT/InvIT must comprise completed, revenue-generating properties/infrastructure projects that have yielded positive cash flows for more than one year.
  • Aggregate Lending & Exposure Limits: • Aggregate Bank Exposure Cap: Total lending across all commercial banks to any single borrowing REIT or InvIT (including its SPVs and holding companies) must not exceed 49% of the value of the trust's total assets. • Funding Restriction: Bank loans to REITs/InvITs cannot be utilized to fund underlying Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) that are already facing financial distress or have existing non-performing loans with regulated entities.
  • Risk Weights & Governance: • Exposure to REITs attracts a 100% risk weight (125% if categorized as capital market exposure). • Exposure to InvITs attracts corporate lending risk weights based on external credit ratings. • Board-approved policies mandatory; statutory migration to a comprehensive capital charge framework effective 1 April 2027.
  • Statutory Effective Date: Directions take effect from 1 October 2026 (banks permitted voluntary early adoption).
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Aggregate Exposure Cap: ≤49% of the value of the trust's total assets (NOT 50% or 75%).
  • Completed Asset Requirement: Minimum 80% completed and revenue-generating with >1 year positive cash flow.
  • Capital Charge Migration Date: 1 April 2027; General compliance effective 1 October 2026.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 5

RBI Master Directions on Authorisation of Payment System Operators (PSOs) — Perpetual Licences & Governance

  • Statutory Authority: Issued under Section 4 of the Payment and Settlement Systems (PSS) Act, 2007, governing entities seeking to operate payment systems in India.
  • Perpetual Validity Regime: • All fresh Certificates of Authorisation (CoA) granted to PSOs will carry perpetual validity (eliminating the earlier 5-year periodic renewal requirement). • Existing authorized PSOs will be transitioned to perpetual validity at the time of their next renewal, subject to complete regulatory compliance. • Non-Compliant Entities: PSOs exhibiting governance or operational deficiencies will receive conditional renewals for a limited period of 1 year only, until deficiencies are fully rectified.
  • FDI & Foreign Investment from FATF Non-Compliant Jurisdictions: • Investments from jurisdictions non-compliant with Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards will not be treated at par with compliant countries. • Fresh investments from FATF non-compliant jurisdictions must account for less than 20% of the voting power of the PSO in aggregate.
  • Surrender of Certificate & Cooling-Off Period: • Surrendering a CoA requires a written application to DPSS Central Office, accompanied by a Statutory Auditor's certificate confirming all customer, merchant, and bank liabilities are fully settled. • A mandatory one-year cooling-off period is imposed before an entity can re-apply if its CoA was revoked, renewal was rejected, or licence was surrendered.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Licence Validity: Perpetual validity for compliant PSOs; 1 year only for non-compliant entities.
  • FATF Non-Compliant Voting Cap: Must remain strictly below 20% of aggregate voting power.
  • Cooling-Off Duration: 1 year from revocation, surrender, or application rejection.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 6

RBI Master Directions on Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) 2026 & Mandatory CERSAI Registration

  • Framework Objective: Comprehensive overhaul of the 2014 TReDS guidelines to accelerate MSME invoice monetization, expand participant categories, and eliminate duplicate factoring frauds.
  • Net Worth Requirement & Transition Timeline: • Minimum Net Worth for new entities seeking TReDS platform authorization fixed at ₹25 crore (verified by statutory auditor certificate, maintained continuously). • Existing authorized TReDS platforms must ramp up their net worth to ₹25 crore by 31 March 2028 (extended compliance horizon).
  • Expanded Market Participants: • Platform now formally accommodates: MSME Sellers, Corporate/PSU/Government Buyers, Financers (Banks, NBFC-Factors, DFIs), Insurance Companies (for credit risk cover), and notified Credit Guarantee Fund Trusts.
  • Mandatory CERSAI Registration: • Every assignment of receivables executed on a TReDS platform must be mandatorily registered with the Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India (CERSAI) to legally prevent multiple discounting of the same invoice across different financiers.
  • Re-Discounting Facility: Authorizes secondary market re-discounting of discounted factoring units between eligible financiers to facilitate liquidity optimization.
  • Current Approved TReDS Platforms (5 entities):
    1. Receivables Exchange of India Limited (RXIL) — India's first operational platform (commenced 9 January 2017).
    2. M1xchange (Mynd Solutions Pvt. Ltd.).
    3. Invoicemart (A.TREDS Ltd. – Axis Bank & mjunction).
    4. C2treds (C2FO Factoring Solutions Pvt. Ltd.).
    5. DTX (KredX Platform Pvt. Ltd.).
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • TReDS Minimum Net Worth: ₹25 crore; Existing platforms must comply by 31 March 2028.
  • Fraud Prevention Registry: Mandatory registration of assigned receivables with CERSAI.
  • First Live Platform: RXIL (commenced operations 9 January 2017).
  • Total RBI-Approved Platforms: 5 platforms as of June 2026.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 7

RBI Revamped Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme Directions 2026: Collateral-Free Limit Raised to ₹2 Lakh

  • Comprehensive Overhaul: RBI issued the Reserve Bank of India (Kisan Credit Card – KCC) Directions, 2026, applying to all Scheduled Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, RRBs, and Rural Co-operative Banks, taking effect from 1 January 2027 (existing loans continue till maturity/renewal).
  • Enhanced Collateral-Free Exemption Limit: • Banks mandated to waive collateral security and margin requirements for agricultural loans up to ₹2 lakh per borrower (raised from the earlier ₹1.60 lakh threshold). • Exemption equally covers allied agricultural activities (dairy, poultry, fisheries, animal husbandry). • Voluntary pledge of gold/silver ornaments for loans up to ₹2 lakh is permitted and will not be treated as a violation of collateral-free guidelines. • KCC loans up to ₹3 lakh secured via hypothecation of crops or assets under formal tie-up recovery arrangements may also be exempted from collateral.
  • Standardized Crop Seasons: • Short-duration crops: Standardized strictly to 12 months (period from raising crop to harvesting and marketing). • Long-duration crops: Standardized strictly to 18 months.
  • Flexi KCC for Marginal Farmers: • Revolving credit facility between ₹10,000 to ₹50,000 designed for marginal farmers (landholding up to 1 hectare) based on land and cropping pattern, without requiring complex cost-of-cultivation documentation.
  • Term Loan Component Repayment Horizon: • Investment credit/term loan portion under KCC is repayable within a maximum of 6 years (if asset life/repayment requires >6 years, it must be treated as a separate loan facility outside KCC).
  • Maximum Permissible Limit (MPL): • Sanctioned limit based on scale of finance + 10% for post-harvest/household + 20% for maintenance/repairs. • For 2nd crop season onwards, MPL is notionally increased by 10% per annum over the previous crop season's limit.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Collateral-Free Limit: ₹2 lakh per borrower (enhanced from ₹1.60 lakh).
  • Standardized Crop Seasons: Short-duration = 12 months; Long-duration = 18 months.
  • Term Loan Under KCC: Maximum repayment tenor 6 years (longer loans must sit outside KCC).
  • Flexi KCC Limits: ₹10,000 to ₹50,000 for marginal farmers (holding ≤1 hectare).
  • Effective Date: 1 January 2027.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 8

RBI Revamps Lead Bank Scheme (LBS): 60% CD Ratio Benchmark & 3-Tier Governance

  • Framework Background: RBI issued revised comprehensive guidelines for the Lead Bank Scheme (LBS) (first introduced in 1969 following the Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee recommendations).
  • Key Administrative Designations: • Lead District Manager (LDM): Lead Bank must appoint an exclusive officer as LDM for each designated district (assignment of multiple districts to one LDM barred except in exceptional circumstances). • District Development Manager (DDM): Appointed by NABARD in every district to liaise between district administration and financial institutions. • Lead District Officer (LDO): Appointed by the Reserve Bank of India for each district to supervise credit flow. • SLBC Convenor: Convenor bank in every State/UT must designate an officer not below the rank of General Manager (GM) as SLBC Convenor.
  • Three-Tier Governance Structure:
    1. Tier 1 (Block Level): Block Level Bankers' Committees (BLBCs).
    2. Tier 2 (District Level): District Consultative Committees (DCCs) and District Level Review Committees (DLRCs).
    3. Tier 3 (State Level): State Level Bankers' Committees (SLBCs / UTLBCs).
  • Credit-Deposit (CD) Ratio Benchmarks & Corrective Action: • Baseline Target: Minimum 60% CD Ratio for rural and semi-urban branches on an all-India basis. • CD Ratio between 40% and 60%: Monitored by the District Consultative Committee (DCC) for step-up improvement. • CD Ratio below 40%: Mandatorily reviewed by a Special Sub-Committee (SSC) under DCC, chaired by the District Collector with LDM as Convenor. • CD Ratio below 20%: District placed under the Special Category Districts for rigorous monthly monitoring and structural intervention. • Similar Special Sub-Committees constituted if Annual Credit Plan (ACP) achievement falls below 100%.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • CD Ratio Thresholds: Ideal target = 60%; Special Sub-Committee review triggered at <40%; Special Category status triggered at <20%.
  • Rank of SLBC Convenor: Not below General Manager (GM).
  • Lead Bank Inception: Introduced in 1969 based on Nariman Committee / F.K.F. Nariman recommendations.
DISPATCH № 9

DFS Launches Common Landing Portal for Unclaimed Financial Assets & UDGAM Convergence

  • Nationwide Campaign: Department of Financial Services (DFS), Ministry of Finance launched the Common Landing Portal for Unclaimed Financial Assets anchored around the national theme: "आपकी पूँजी, आपका अधिकार" (Your Money, Your Right).
  • Institutional Integration: Integrates cross-sector unclaimed funds across multiple regulators into a unified citizen-facing interface: • Bank Deposits: RBI's UDGAM portal (Unclaimed Deposits – Gateway to Access inforMation), linking inactive accounts (10+ years) transferred to the DEA Fund (Depositor Education and Awareness Fund, Sec 26A BRA 1949). • Dividends & Corporate Shares: IEPFA (Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority under Ministry of Corporate Affairs). • Insurance Dues: Bima Bharosa / IRDAI unclaimed policyholders' ledger. • Mutual Funds & Pensions: SEBI / PFRDA centralized tracing engines.
  • Search Capability: Centralized search across multiple banking and financial institutions using PAN, Name, Mobile Number, and Aadhaar-authenticated digital KYC.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Campaign Slogan: "आपकी पूँजी, आपका अधिकार" (Your Money, Your Right).
  • Inactive Account Transfer Horizon: Savings/Current/FD inactive for 10 years or more transferred to DEA Fund.
  • UDGAM Full Form: Unclaimed Deposits – Gateway to Access inforMation.

RBI Annual Report 2025–26: Balance Sheet Surges 20.6% to ₹91.97 Lakh Crore & ₹2.89 Lakh Crore Surplus Transfer

  • Statutory Submission: Submitted by the Central Board of Directors of the Reserve Bank of India to the Central Government under Section 53(2) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (reporting period: April 2025 – March 2026).
  • Balance Sheet Expansion: • Total balance sheet size expanded by 20.6% (an absolute increase of ₹15,71,699.15 crore), rising from ₹76,25,421.93 crore as on March 31, 2025 to ₹91,97,121.08 crore as on March 31, 2026. • Balance Sheet-to-GDP Ratio: Stood at 26.4% of India's GDP as of end-March 2026 (up from 23.7% a year ago). • Initial paid-up capital of the Reserve Bank remains at ₹5 crore (constituted as a private shareholders bank in 1935, fully nationalised on January 1, 1949).
  • Surplus Transfer & Contingent Risk Buffer (CRB): • Surplus Transfer to Central Government: RBI approved a total surplus transfer of ₹2,88,588.45 crore (₹2.89 lakh crore) for FY26 (up 7.3% from ₹2,68,588.07 crore in FY25). Total available balance was ₹2,88,592.45 crore (with ₹4 crore statutory contributions: ₹1 crore each to National Industrial Credit Long Term Operations Fund, National Housing Credit LTO Fund, and ₹1 crore each transferable to NABARD for National Rural Credit LTO Fund and National Rural Credit Stabilisation Fund). • Economic Capital Framework (ECF / Bimal Jalan Committee): Mandates CRB within 4.5% to 7.5% of balance sheet. The Central Board approved maintaining the CRB at the upper cap of 6.5%. • Contingency Fund (CF) Allocation: RBI made a provision of ₹1,09,379.64 crore (~₹1.09 lakh crore) transferred to CF during the year. No provision was made towards Asset Development Fund (ADF).
  • Asset Composition & Financial Performance: • Total Income: Increased by 26.4%, while total expenditure rose by 102.4%. • Foreign Assets (70.9%): Foreign investments rose 7.9% to ₹52.68 lakh crore; sovereign gold holdings jumped 63.8% to ₹10.94 lakh crore. Net sale of foreign exchange stood at USD 53.13 billion, yielding net exchange gains of ₹1.69 lakh crore. • Domestic Assets (29.1%): Rose 44.9% to ₹22.59 lakh crore. Rupee securities interest income grew 37.7% to ₹1.18 lakh crore. • Liabilities Breakdown: Revaluation accounts (+63.4%), Notes issued (+11.8%), Deposits (+11.6%), Other liabilities (+21.1%).
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Total Balance Sheet Size: ₹91,97,121.08 crore (+20.6% YoY growth; 26.4% of GDP).
  • Surplus Transferred to GoI: ₹2,88,588.45 crore (FY25: ₹2,68,588.07 crore).
  • Provision to Contingency Fund (CF): ₹1,09,379.64 crore (CRB pegged at 6.5%; ECF band: 4.5%–7.5%).
  • Section Applied: Section 53(2) for Annual Report submission; initial capital remains ₹5 crore (nationalised Jan 1, 1949).

RBI Annual Report 2025–26: Currency Management, Counterfeits (FICNs) & Digital Rupee (e₹)

  • Banknotes & Coins in Circulation: • Banknotes in Circulation (BiC): Increased by 11.9% in value and 10.5% in volume during 2025–26. • Highest Denomination Share: In volume terms, the ₹500 denomination constituted the highest share of total banknotes in circulation, followed by the ₹10 denomination. • Coins in Circulation: Total value increased by 11.4%, while volume expanded by 4.5%. Coins of ₹1, ₹2, and ₹5 together constituted 80.7% of total volume and 60.2% of total value. • ₹2000 Note Withdrawal Status: As of March 31, 2026, 98.45% of the ₹3.56 lakh crore worth of ₹2000 banknotes in circulation at the time of the withdrawal announcement (May 19, 2023) had returned to the banking system. Facility remains active across 19 RBI Issue Offices.
  • Central Bank Digital Currency (e₹): • Total e₹ (CBDC) in circulation stood at ₹771.7 crore as on March 31, 2026. • Retail programmable CBDC pilots successfully credited food subsidies to Public Distribution System (PDS) beneficiaries across Gujarat, Puducherry, and Chandigarh. • RBI launched the Unified Markets Interface (UMI) to facilitate tokenisation of financial assets using wholesale CBDC (first pilot launched on Certificates of Deposit - CDs). • Bilateral cross-border CBDC discussions/MoUs held with Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Central Bank of the UAE (CBUAE); joined BIS Innovation Hub's Project Rialto and Project Mandala (Phase 2).
  • Counterfeit Currency (FICNs) Detection: • Share of Detection: Only 2.4% of total Fake Indian Currency Notes (FICNs) detected across the banking sector were detected at the Reserve Bank of India; 97.6% were detected by commercial banks. • Denomination Trends: Counterfeit notes detected in ₹10, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, and ₹2000 denominations registered a marked decline; counterfeit ₹500 notes increased by 20.5% and ₹20 notes increased by 47.4%. • Currency Infrastructure & Awareness: State Bank of India (SBI) accounted for the highest share of Currency Chests across India. RBI replaced its legacy 'Paisa Bolta Hai' portal with the comprehensive Indian Currency Microsite on September 10, 2025. Print trials of varnished banknotes were conducted at BRBNMPL Mysuru Press.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Total CBDC (e₹) in Circulation: ₹771.7 crore (as of March 31, 2026).
  • ₹2000 Note Return Rate: 98.45% of ₹3.56 lakh crore total value returned.
  • FICN Detection Share: Reserve Bank detected 2.4%; Commercial Banks detected 97.6%.
  • Banknote Value/Volume Growth: Value grew 11.9%; Volume grew 10.5% (₹500 note leads volume share).
  • Largest Currency Chest Holder: State Bank of India (SBI).

RBI Annual Report 2025–26: Bank Frauds, Supervisory Reforms & Regulatory Modernisation

  • Systemic Fraud Surge: • Total fraud amount surged 46% to ₹48,021 crore in 2025–26 (from ₹32,803 crore in FY25), even as total reported fraud incidents fell by more than half to 10,114 cases. • Public Sector Banks (PSBs): Accounted for 74.5% of total fraud value (₹35,709 crore across 3,000+ cases; average fraud size ₹6.6 crore). • Private Sector Banks: Accounted for 23.7% (₹11,399 crore). • Dominant Segment: Loan Advances accounted for 85% of total fraud value (₹40,774 crore across 8,640 cases).
  • Consolidation of Regulations Exercise: • To streamline compliance, more than 11,000 circulars and instructions were consolidated into 244 Master Directions (MDs) covering 30 functional areas across 11 classes of Regulated Entities (REs), repealing 9,445 circulars. • RBI also released 64 draft master directions across 9 functional supervisory areas.
  • Deposit Insurance & Supervisory Governance: • DICGC Premium: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (established under DICGC Act, 1961) maintained a flat-rate premium of ₹0.12 (12 paise) per ₹100 per annum (0.12% p.a.) on assessable deposits; coverage limit intact at ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank. • Risk-Based Premium (RBP) Framework: Introduced effective April 1, 2026, establishing a 2-tier risk-based rating methodology (Tier 1: SCBs other than RRBs; Tier 2: RRBs, rural co-op banks, and UCBs). • Registered Insured Banks: Stood at 1,950 as of March 31, 2026 (124 commercial banks including 11 SFBs, 6 PBs, 28 RRBs, 2 LABs; and 1,826 co-operative banks). • Supervisory Data Quality Index (sDQI): Published on a quarterly basis under Utkarsh 2.0. • Co-Lending Framework Revision: Reduced minimum loan share retention by Regulated Entities from 20% to 10%, and extended First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG) coverage up to 5%.
  • AI Governance & FinTech Architecture: • FREE-AI Framework: RBI formulated the Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence anchored on 7 Sutras and 6 Strategic Pillars (26 recommendations: 13 on innovation enablement, 13 on risk mitigation). • MuleHunter.ai™: AI/ML supervised model developed by RBI Innovation Hub (RBIH) to identify mule bank accounts in near-real time. • Digital Payment Intelligence Platform (DPIP): Established as a collaborative network-level digital intelligence utility to combat payment fraud.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Consolidation of Regulations: 11,000+ circulars condensed into 244 Master Directions; 9,445 repealed.
  • DICGC Flat Premium: 0.12% per annum (12 paise per ₹100); RBP framework effective April 1, 2026.
  • Co-Lending Retention Minimum: Lowered to 10% (FLDG cover up to 5%).
  • FREE-AI Architecture: 7 Sutras + 6 Pillars + 26 Recommendations; Mule detector = MuleHunter.ai™.
  • Total System Frauds: ₹48,021 crore (PSBs = 74.5%; Advances = ₹40,774 crore / 85%).

RBI Annual Report 2025–26: Monetary Operations, Payment Systems & Organisational Milestones

  • Monetary Policy Operations & Corridors: • Policy Corridor: Retained a symmetric policy corridor of 50 bps around the policy repo rate (SDF at -25 bps, MSF at +25 bps). • Call Money & Repo Market Timings: Call money market trading hours extended to 7:00 PM (effective July 1, 2025; 9:00 AM – 7:00 PM); tri-party and market repo extended to 4:00 PM (effective August 1, 2025). • Liquidity Stance: Average daily net absorption under LAF rose to ₹1.86 lakh crore (from ₹1,605 crore in FY25); SDF accounted for 84.9% (₹2.02 lakh crore) of total absorption. WACR spread averaged (-) 7 bps below the repo rate. • External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR): As of December 2025, EBLR-linked loans accounted for 50.6% of floating-rate loans at Public Sector Banks and 89.2% at Private Sector Banks.
  • Payment & Settlement Infrastructure: • UPI Volume & Dominance: UPI volume surged 30% YoY, crossing 200 billion transactions; UPI's share in total retail payment transactions reached 86%. • Global UPI Footprint: QR-code merchant acceptance operational in 8 countries (Bhutan, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Qatar, Singapore, Sri Lanka, and the UAE). • NGRTGS Upgraded to Version 4.0: Built on the international ISO 20022 XML messaging standard; RTGS transaction volume grew 15.7% (value rose 12.9%). • Banking Web Domains: Under Phase 1, bank websites mandated to migrate to exclusive .bank.in domains by October 31, 2025. • Cheque Clearing Centralisation: Inward clearing centralised by setting up a national service branch at Chennai Regional Office, replacing decentralised operations across 19 ROs. • PRAVAAH Portal: Centralised web portal for regulatory approvals and licensing processed over 90%+ digitised flows.
  • Organisational & Institutional Governance: • Utkarsh 2029: Reserve Bank adopted its next medium-term strategy framework covering a 3-year horizon (2026–29) across 6 strategic pillars. • Leadership Changes: Shri Shirish Chandra Murmu appointed Deputy Governor succeeding Shri M. Rajeshwar Rao (tenure completed October 8, 2025); Ms. Anuradha Thakur nominated Central Board Director succeeding Shri Ajay Seth (July 24, 2025). • Public Engagement: Launched official podcast series 'RBI Talks: From Paisa to Policy' on January 1, 2026 (debut episode on KYC). Nationwide public awareness tagline: "RBI Kehta Hai... Smart Bano, Cool Raho". • Training & Infrastructure: Reserve Bank Staff College (RBSC) located in Chennai; College of Agricultural Banking (CAB) in Pune; College of Supervisors (CoS) in Mumbai; ECCTI in Bhubaneswar.

RBI 61st MPC Meeting (June 2026): Repo Rate Held at 5.25% with Neutral Stance

  • Monetary Policy Review: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) conducted its 61st meeting (2nd Bi-Monthly Meeting of FY 2026-27), chaired by RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra.
  • Policy Rates Decision: • Policy Repo Rate: Kept unchanged at 5.25% under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF). • Standing Deposit Facility (SDF): Unchanged at 5.00% (25 bps below repo rate). • Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) & Bank Rate: Unchanged at 5.50% (25 bps above repo rate). • Reserve Ratios: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) maintained at 3.00%; Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) at 18.00%; Fixed Reverse Repo Rate at 3.35%.

RBI Introduces Special USD-Rupee Forex Swap Facilities to Attract Capital Inflows

  • Twin Forex Swap Windows: To stabilize the Rupee against crude oil volatility and encourage foreign currency inflows, RBI introduced two concessional USD-INR forex swap facilities:
    1. FCNR(B) Window: For fresh Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank [FCNR(B)] deposits of 3 to 5 years maturity.
    2. ECB/OFCB Window: For fresh External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) and Overseas Foreign Currency Borrowings (OFCBs) raised by AD Category-I banks (maturity ≥3 years).
  • Concessional Pricing & Tenor: • Fixed Swap Rate: Swaps executed at a fixed rate of 1.5% per annum (compounded semi-annually), significantly below prevailing market hedging rates. • Tenor: Aligned with borrowing maturity, capped at a maximum of 5 years. • Operational Windows: FCNR(B) swap window open till 16 October 2026 (deposits mobilized up to 30 Sept 2026); ECB/OFCB window open till 15 January 2027 (inflows up to 31 Dec 2026).
  • Statutory Reserve Exemptions & NOP-INR Relief: • Eligible FCNR(B) deposits mobilized under this scheme are exempt from CRR (3.0%) and SLR (18.0%) requirements. • RBI exempted swap positions from Net Open Position in Rupee (NOP-INR) limits (which restricts banks' onshore deliverable positions to USD 100 million at end of day), allowing banks to swap up to hundreds of millions without breaching exposure caps.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Fixed Swap Rate: 1.5% per annum compounded semi-annually.
  • Statutory Exemptions: Fresh FCNR(B) deposits under the scheme are exempt from CRR and SLR.
  • NOP-INR Rule: Banks are normally subject to a $100 million Net Open Position deliverable cap, which is waived for these swaps.

Ministry of Finance & RBI Reform FPI Debt Framework: Capital Gains Exemption & PROI Limit Hike

  • Income-Tax Exemption on Sovereign Debt: • Central Government notified that tax liability for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs/FIIs) on specified Government Securities (G-Secs) investments is reduced to Nil effective 1 April 2026. • Both interest income and capital gains (earlier Short-Term Capital Gains taxed at 30%, Long-Term at 12.5%) earned from specified G-Secs are completely exempt from tax. • Similar comprehensive tax exemption extended to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
  • Liberalisation for Persons Resident Outside India (PROI): • Permitted individual Persons Resident Outside India (PROIs) (including non-NRIs/OCIs) to invest in listed Indian equity through the Portfolio Investment Scheme (PIS). • Individual Limit: Increased from 5% to 10% of the paid-up equity capital of an Indian company. • Aggregate Limit: Increased from 10% to 24% for all PROIs combined.
  • FPI Limits under General Route Rationalized: • Short-term investment limit (earlier capped at 30% for securities with residual maturity up to 1 year) completely removed. • Concentration limits (earlier 10% to 15% per corporate debt issuer) completely removed. • Retained quantitative sovereign caps: 6.0% of outstanding stock in Central G-Secs and 2.0% in State Development Loans (SDLs).
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • FPI G-Sec Tax Rate: Reduced to Nil from 1 April 2026 (both interest and capital gains).
  • PROI Equity Investment Caps: Individual limit raised to 10% (from 5%); Aggregate limit raised to 24% (from 10%).
  • FPI G-Sec Stock Caps: 6% for Central Government Securities, 2% for SDLs.

CAPITAL MARKETS & REGULATORY № 23

SEBI Revises Trading Framework for ETFs: Dynamic Price Bands & Pre-Open Auction

  • Regulatory Directive: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) revamped the trading framework for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs), taking effect from 1 September 2026, replacing the rigid 20% fixed NAV price band.
  • Dynamic Price Band Architecture: • Equity & Debt ETFs: Initial dynamic price band set at 10%. If touched, a cooling-off period is triggered, followed by phased expansions in increments of 5% up to a maximum of 20%. • Overnight & Liquid ETFs: Completely excluded from dynamic price bands.
  • Commodity ETFs (Gold & Silver ETFs): • Initial dynamic price band set at ±6%. • Expandable in stages of 3% following a cooling-off period, with no upper or lower limit on total price expansions during a trading session to mirror global bullion market volatility.
  • Base Price Determination via VWAP: • ETF base price determined using the Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP) of trades executed during the last 30 minutes of the previous trading day.
  • Pre-Open Call Auction Mechanism: • Introduced a dedicated Pre-Open Call Auction session specifically for commodity ETFs to ensure fair price discovery prior to regular market open.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Initial Dynamic Price Bands: 10% for Equity/Debt ETFs (max 20%); ±6% for Commodity Gold/Silver ETFs (expandable by 3%, no cap).
  • Excluded Categories: Overnight and Liquid ETFs.
  • Base Price Formula: VWAP of the last 30 minutes of trading.
  • Effective Date: 1 September 2026.

PFRDA Eases NPS Annuity Exit Rules & Launches 'StAR NPS' Digital Onboarding Platform

  • Exit Relaxation in NPS Annuities: • Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) relaxed rigid lifetime lock-in norms for annuity contracts purchased under the National Pension System (NPS). • Surrender for Hardship: Annuity Service Providers (ASPs) are now permitted to allow surrender of annuity policies in exceptional hardship cases, specifically where the annuitant or an immediate family member is diagnosed with a critical illness. • Pre-October 2024 Policies: Applies to annuity products issued prior to 24 October 2024 provided the contract contained an underlying surrender clause. • Reporting to CRA: ASPs must report all approved annuity surrender cases to the Central Recordkeeping Agency (CRA) within 7 working days.
  • Launch of 'StAR NPS' Digital Assisted Onboarding: • PFRDA introduced 'StAR NPS', a cutting-edge assisted digital onboarding platform developed by BSE Technologies Private Limited (BTPL). • Facilitates instant 12-digit Permanent Retirement Account Number (PRAN) generation through real-time CRA integration, Central KYC (CKYC), and DigiLocker. • Open to Indian residents aged 18 to 85 years; Onboarding fee of ₹200 per subscriber borne by the respective Point of Presence (PoP).
  • PFRDA Regulatory Sandbox Framework: • Operationalized from 2 June 2026 to enable controlled live testing of innovative pension tech solutions. • Eligible applicants include registered intermediaries, fintech firms, and LLPs with a minimum net worth of ₹10 lakh. • Mandatory reporting: Monthly progress reports, plus any fraud incident or financial loss must be reported within 24 hours.

MNRE Operationalizes Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India (GHCI)

  • Framework & Institutional Mandate: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) operationalized the Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India (GHCI) under the National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM), establishing the nation's statutory standard for green hydrogen accounting.
  • Emission & Quality Benchmark: • Green Hydrogen is defined as hydrogen produced through water electrolysis or biomass conversion with well-to-gate greenhouse gas emissions not exceeding 2 kg CO2 equivalent per kg of H2 (<2.0 kg CO2 eq/kg H2), calculated as an average over a 12-month period.
  • Mission Targets by 2030: • Achieve an annual production capacity of at least 5 MMT (Million Metric Tonnes) of green hydrogen. • Deploy 125 GW of associated renewable energy capacity. • Mobilize over ₹8 Lakh Crore in total investments and create over 600,000 clean energy jobs. • Abate approximately 50 MMT of annual carbon dioxide emissions.
  • Implementation & State Adoption: • Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) functions as the Nodal Authority for accreditation and certification. • Dedicated Policy States (6): Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Gujarat, and Uttarakhand. • Integrated Policy States (6): Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh, and Assam.

DISPATCH № 42

WPI Base Year Revision to 2022-23: DPIIT Introduces Targeted Mean Imputation for Missing Prices

  • Statistical Modernization: Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce & Industry) finalized the methodology for transitioning the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) from the 2011-12 base to the new 2022-23 base year.
  • Methodological Breakthrough: • Replaces the legacy "Carry Forward" method (which duplicated the previous month's price when data was missing) with "Targeted Mean Imputation". • Imputes missing commodity quotations using the weighted average price trend of closely related items within the same commodity group, eliminating artificial price stickiness.
  • May 2026 Inflation Readings: • Headline WPI inflation recorded at 9.68% (all-India Index at 109.9). • WPI Food Index inflation stood at 4.49%.

  • New WPI Target Base Year: 2022-23 (replacing 2011-12).

DISPATCH № 1

DFS Approves Viability Plan 2.0 for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) Across 30 Performance Metrics

  • Regulatory Framework & Mandate: The Department of Financial Services (DFS), Ministry of Finance, formally approved the operationalization of Viability Plan 2.0 for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) across India.
  • Tenure & Multi-Year Horizon: • Extends structured performance monitoring for a period of three financial years: spanning from FY 2025-26 (FY26) to FY 2027-28 (FY28). • Builds upon the foundation of Viability Plan 1.0 (which governed RRB turnaround between FY 2021-22 and FY 2024-25).
  • Comprehensive 30-Parameter Assessment Matrix: • Evaluates institutional health across 30 standardized performance parameters categorized into four core pillars:
    1. Operational Excellence: Branch productivity, digital banking penetration, and financial inclusion outreach.
    2. Asset Quality: Reduction in Gross and Net Non-Performing Assets (NPAs), provision coverage ratios (PCR), and slippage containment.
    3. Profitability & Capital: Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR), Return on Assets (RoA), Net Interest Margin (NIM), and cost-to-income efficiency.
    4. Credit Expansion: Credit-Deposit (CD) ratio alignment, Priority Sector Lending (PSL) target compliance, and saturation under central flagship schemes (PM-Kisan, PMJDY, PMJJBY, PMSBY).
  • Strategic Governance Rationale: Institutionalizes quarterly monitoring committees comprising Sponsor Bank representatives, NABARD officials, and state finance secretaries to ensure sustainable, self-reliant rural credit delivery without perpetual recapitalization infusions.

  • Statutory Pricing Mandate: The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA), chaired by the Prime Minister, approved the Minimum Support Prices (MSP) for 14 mandated Kharif crops for Marketing Season 2026–27.
  • Key Mandated Crop Prices (per quintal): • Common Paddy: Fixed at ₹2,441 per quintal (Grade 'A' Paddy fixed at ₹2,461 per quintal). • Coarse Grains: Maize at ₹2,410 per quintal; Bajra at ₹2,625 per quintal; Jowar (Hybrid) at ₹3,371 per quintal; Ragi at ₹4,290 per quintal. • Pulses: • Tur / Arhar: Fixed at ₹8,450 per quintal. • Moong: Fixed at ₹8,780 per quintal. • Urad: Fixed at ₹8,200 per quintal. • Oilseeds: • Sunflower Seed: Fixed at ₹8,343 per quintal. • Soybean (Yellow): Fixed at ₹5,708 per quintal. • Groundnut: Fixed at ₹6,783 per quintal. • Sesamum: Fixed at ₹9,267 per quintal. • Nigerseed: Fixed at ₹8,717 per quintal. • Cotton: Medium Staple Cotton fixed at ₹8,267 per quintal; Long Staple Cotton fixed at ₹8,667 per quintal.

Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026: Lok Sabha Strength Proposed to Expand to 850 Members

  • Legislative Restructuring: The Union Government introduced The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-First Amendment) Bill, 2026, initiating historic constitutional changes to the composition of the House of the People (Lok Sabha).
  • Substantive Increase in House Strength: • Proposes expanding the sanctioned statutory strength of the Lok Sabha from 543 to 850 members. • Article 81 Modification: • Up to a maximum of 815 members to be directly elected from territorial constituencies across the States of India. • Up to 35 members to represent the Union Territories. • Total Proposed Capacity: 850 Members.
  • Removal of the Post-2026 Delimitation Freeze (Article 82): • Under the 84th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2001, the readjustment of territorial constituencies (delimitation) was frozen until the figures of the first Census taken after the year 2026 were published. • The 131st Amendment Bill removes this strict temporal freeze, permitting the immediate initiation of delimitation based on updated census data.
  • Catalyst for Women's Reservation: Facilitates the operationalization and seat-allocation mechanism required under the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam), which mandates reserving 33% of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies following the delimitation exercise.

BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 12

RBI Deregulates FinTech Cross-Border Outward Remittances: Removes Prior Approval Mandate

  • Framework Liberalisation: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) discontinued the mandate requiring Authorised Dealer Category-I (AD Cat-I) banks to obtain prior approval from the central bank before entering into tie-up arrangements with non-bank entities (including FinTechs) for outward cross-border remittances.
  • Applicability & Scope: • Applies strictly to Cross-Border Outward Remittance of funds for Non-Trade Current Account Transactions. • Covers digital applications, web portals, and software platforms operated by third-party FinTech entities facilitating customer-facing remittances.
  • Mandatory Bank Compliance & Transparency Safeguards: • Statutory Adherence: AD Cat-I banks remain entirely responsible for strict compliance under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) and Master Directions on Know Your Customer (KYC) / AML. • Full Customer Disclosure: Banks must clearly disclose to the remitter:
    1. The exact foreign exchange amount that will be credited into the overseas beneficiary's account.
    2. The maximum expected time required for the funds to reach the beneficiary. • Prevents opaque hidden markups, intermediary bank deductions, and arbitrary foreign exchange conversion spreads.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Regulatory Shift: Prior RBI approval requirement removed for AD Cat-I bank tie-ups with FinTechs.
  • Permitted Scope: Non-Trade Current Account Transactions only (trade capital accounts excluded).
  • Core Statutory Laws: Governed under FEMA 1999 and RBI KYC Directions.
  • Mandated Disclosures: Exact foreign currency amount and maximum delivery time.

  • Technological Weapon — MuleHunter.ai™: • RBIH developed MuleHunter.ai™, an enterprise AI/ML supervised algorithm designed to detect, tag, and isolate digital mule bank accounts in near-real time. • Mule accounts serve as illicit conduit accounts used by cybercrime syndicates to layer, move, or withdraw fraudulent proceeds.
  • Integration with Digital Payment Intelligence Platform (DPIP): • MuleHunter.ai™ feeds live behavioral intelligence directly into RBI's Digital Payment Intelligence Platform (DPIP) to generate transaction-level fraud probability scores for banks and payment service providers.

BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 14

RBI Revises Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR) Norms: Discontinued for Commercial Banks, Retained for UCBs & RRBs

  • Major Capital & Prudential Shift: Reserve Bank of India issued final amendment directions revising the regulatory architecture for Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR), effective May 18, 2026.
  • Commercial Banks (CBs) & Foreign Banks (FBs): • IFR Requirement Discontinued: RBI officially discontinued the mandatory IFR requirement for Commercial Banks and Foreign Banks, noting that modern Basel capital adequacy ratios and risk-management norms already provide sufficient loss absorption against bond mark-to-market (MTM) depreciation. • Treatment of Existing IFR Balances: Existing IFR balances as of May 17, 2026, must be transferred "below the line" to either the Statutory Reserve, the General Reserve, or the Profit and Loss Account. • Tier 1 Capital Reclassification: Transferred balances are now recognized as Tier 1 (Core Capital), boosting banks' core capitalization metrics. • Foreign Bank Branches: Balances transferred directly to "statutory reserve kept in Indian books" or "remittable surplus retained in Indian books" (non-repatriable while Indian operations continue).
  • Provisions for PBs, SFBs, RRBs & Co-operative Banks: • Relaxation for Balance Sheet Frequency: Payments Banks (PBs), Small Finance Banks (SFBs), and Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) are now required to maintain the prescribed IFR level only on balance sheet dates (rather than continuously throughout the year). • Target Threshold: PBs, SFBs, and RRBs must maintain an IFR of at least 2% of the Available for Sale (AFS) and Fair Value Through Profit and Loss (FVTPL / HFT) portfolios, eligible for Tier 2 Capital. • Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) & Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs): Must continue to maintain a minimum IFR of 5% of their investment portfolio; excess amounts over 5% may be transferred to the Profit and Loss Account at the end of the accounting year; qualifies for Tier 2 Capital.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Effective Date: May 18, 2026.
  • Commercial Banks Status: IFR requirement completely discontinued; existing balances qualify as Tier 1 Capital.
  • SFBs, PBs & RRBs Norm: Maintained only on balance sheet dates; minimum 2% of AFS/FVTPL; qualifies as Tier 2 Capital.
  • Co-operative Banks (UCBs/RCBs): Minimum IFR remains 5% of investment portfolio (Tier 2 Capital).
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 15

RBI Discussion Paper on Digital Payment Safety: 1-Hour Lagged Credit, Kill Switch & ₹25 Lakh Annual Cap

  • Combating Authorized Push Payment (APP) Frauds: RBI released a comprehensive Discussion Paper outlining high-friction security interventions to protect retail depositors against social engineering, digital arrest, and APP cyber frauds (which inflicted ₹22,930 crore losses in 2025).
  • 1-Hour Lagged Credit on High-Value UPI/IMPS: • Proposes a mandatory 1-hour settlement delay for all online digital transfers (UPI, IMPS, NEFT) exceeding ₹10,000. • During this 1-hour escrow window, the sender retains the unilateral legal right to cancel the transaction. • Whitelisting Exemption: Instant real-time settlement permitted without delay if the beneficiary has been pre-registered on the customer's whitelisted trusted beneficiary list. • Empirical Rationale: RBI observed that transactions above ₹10,000 account for 98.5% of total digital fraud value and 45% of reported cyber fraud cases.
  • Trusted Person Authentication for Vulnerable Citizens: • Introduces dual-authorization safeguards for senior citizens aged above 70 years and persons with disabilities (PwDs). • Any digital fund transfer exceeding ₹50,000 will require secondary approval from a pre-nominated trusted family member or guardian.
  • National Digital 'Kill Switch' & Annual Credit Cap: • Universal Kill Switch: Mandates a one-tap emergency Kill Switch across all mobile banking apps to immediately freeze all digital outbound payment channels (modeled on Singapore and Australian protocols). • ₹25 Lakh Annual Credit Limit: Proposes capping aggregate annual credits received by individual and small merchant accounts at ₹25 lakh; excess funds parked in a holding 'shadow balance' pending KYC reverification.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • UPI Lagged Credit Threshold: Transfers above ₹10,000 held for 1 hour (cancellable by sender).
  • Fraud Value Concentration: Above ₹10,000 transfers account for 98.5% of fraud value.
  • Senior Citizen Rule: Transfers above ₹50,000 for citizens >70 years require trusted person sign-off.
  • Annual Credit Cap: ₹25 lakh annual incoming credit cap (shadow balance mechanism).
  • Emergency Mechanism: One-tap Digital Kill Switch.

RBI Rationalises Disaster Relief Loan Restructuring: Suo Motu Automatic Restructuring & 135-Day Opt-Out

  • Framework Notification: Reserve Bank of India issued revised directions empowering commercial banks and non-banking lenders to deliver immediate credit relief to borrowers struck by natural calamities.
  • Automatic Relief & Suo Motu Restructuring: • Lenders permitted to initiate loan restructuring suo motu (without waiting for formal distress applications from borrowers) across areas declared as disaster-hit under the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) or State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF). • Relief measures include lowering loan interest rates, extending repayment tenures, converting short-term crop loans into medium/long-term term loans, and granting moratoriums.
  • 135-Day Borrower Opt-Out Window: • Restructuring applies automatically across all eligible standard loan accounts; affected borrowers are granted a 135-day window from the date of calamity declaration to opt out if they prefer to service existing repayment terms.
  • Eligibility & Asset Classification Safeguards: • Standard Account Rule: Account must be classified as 'Standard' on the date of calamity declaration and not in default for more than 30 days. • Slippage Upgrade: Any account that slips into NPA between the calamity declaration date and restructuring implementation will be upgraded back to 'Standard' upon execution of the relief plan. • Provisioning: Banks must maintain an additional specific provision of 5% on the outstanding debt of restructured borrowers. • Timelines: Plan invocation within 45 days of calamity declaration; full implementation within 90 days thereafter.

  • Pre-Condition Default Cap: Not in default for more than 30 days on calamity date.
  • Provisioning Requirement: Additional 5% specific provision on restructured debt.
  • Implementation Window: Invocation within 45 days; implementation within 90 days.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 17

RBI Mandates Master Direction on Expected Credit Loss (ECL) Framework Effective April 1, 2027

  • Historic Shift in Credit Provisioning: RBI formally issued the comprehensive Master Direction on Expected Credit Loss (ECL) Approach for Bank Loans, superseding the legacy 40-year-old 'Incurred Loss' provisioning model, effective April 1, 2027.
  • Three-Stage Asset Classification & Provisioning Model: • Stage 1 (Low Credit Risk / Normal): • Exposures with low or no significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition. • Provisioning: 12-month Expected Credit Losses (ECL). • Minimum statutory floor: At least 0.40% on secured retail, corporate, and medium enterprise loans; 0.25% on small/micro enterprises and farm credit; 1.00% on unsecured retail loans. • Stage 2 (Significant Increase in Credit Risk - SICR): • Exposures where credit risk has increased significantly since origination, but which are not yet credit-impaired (automatically triggered if payments are overdue by >30 days). • Provisioning: Lifetime Expected Credit Losses (Lifetime ECL). • Minimum statutory floor: 5.00% provisioning across corporate, retail, and unsecured credit. • Stage 3 (Credit-Impaired / NPAs): • Defaulted exposures meeting the statutory 90-day delinquency threshold. • Provisioning: Lifetime ECL (progressively scaling up to 100% for unsecured exposures depending on age of default).
  • Core Statistical Mechanics & Income Recognition: • ECL computed using econometric formula: ECL=Probability of Default (PD)×Loss Given Default (LGD)×Exposure at Default (EAD)\text{ECL} = \text{Probability of Default (PD)} \times \text{Loss Given Default (LGD)} \times \text{Exposure at Default (EAD)}ECL=Probability of Default (PD)×Loss Given Default (LGD)×Exposure at Default (EAD). • Borrower-Level Cross-Contamination: If any single loan facility of a borrower turns NPA, all other credit exposures of that borrower across the bank must be classified as NPA. • Effective Interest Rate (EIR) Transition: Banks mandated to transition their entire loan books to Effective Interest Rate (EIR) accounting by March 31, 2030. • Governance: Supervised by a Board-approved Committee comprising the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and Chief Risk Officer (CRO).
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Effective Enforcement Date: April 1, 2027.
  • Transition Milestone: Full transition to Effective Interest Rate (EIR) by March 31, 2030.
  • Stage 1 Provisioning: 12-Month ECL (0.40% secured, 0.25% MSME/agri, 1.00% unsecured retail).
  • Stage 2 Trigger: Overdue by >30 days; requires Lifetime ECL (minimum 5.00%).
  • Stage 3 Trigger: Overdue by >90 days; requires Lifetime ECL (up to 100%).
  • Quantitative Formula: PD×LGD×EAD\text{PD} \times \text{LGD} \times \text{EAD}PD×LGD×EAD.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 18

RBI Mandates Global Reporting of All Rupee OTC Foreign Exchange Derivatives to CCIL

  • FX Derivatives Transparency Overhaul: Reserve Bank of India instituted a sweeping reporting reform mandating Authorised Dealer Category-I (AD Cat-I) banks to report all Over-the-Counter (OTC) Foreign Exchange (FX) Derivative Contracts involving the Indian Rupee (INR).
  • Reporting Repository & Global Extraterritoriality: • All transactions must be reported to the trade repository of the Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL). • Extends extraterritorially: Covers OTC Rupee derivative contracts executed anywhere in the world by the bank's parent company, overseas branches, and foreign subsidiaries/related entities. • Captures both Deliverable and Non-Deliverable Forward (NDF) contracts.
  • Three-Phase Progressive Implementation Timetable: • Phase 1 (Effective July 1, 2027): Mandatory reporting of 100% of contracts entered into by the parent bank entities. • Phase 2 (Effective January 1, 2028): Reporting of at least 70% of total notional trade value executed by other related entities / overseas arms (progressively stepping up to 80%). • Phase 3 (Effective July 1, 2028): Full compliance mandated — 100% of notional trade value across all global related entities must be reported.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Mandatory Trade Repository: Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL).
  • Phase 1 Deadline: July 1, 2027 (100% of parent entity contracts).
  • Phase 2 Deadline: January 1, 2028 (70%–80% notional value of related entities).
  • Phase 3 Full Enforcement: July 1, 2028 (100% notional value worldwide).
  • Instruments Covered: Both Deliverable and Non-Deliverable OTC Rupee FX Derivatives.

SEBI Introduces 'GARUDA' Green-Channel Fast-Track Mechanism for Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)

  • Reforming Private Capital Formation: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) introduced the GARUDA Mechanism (Green-Channel: Alternative Investment Funds Rollout Upon Document Acknowledgement) to eliminate regulatory delays in launching private investment funds.
  • Radical Reduction in Approval Timelines: • Non-Accredited Investor Schemes: Rollout timeline slashed from the prevailing 30-day waiting period down to within 10 working days of filing the Placement Memorandum (PPM). • Angel Funds & Accredited Investor (AI-only) Schemes: Granted immediate green-channel fundraising clearance upon direct digital filing with SEBI, completely eliminating the requirement to route filings through merchant bankers.
  • Enhanced Accountability & Due Diligence: • Replaces redundant Merchant Banker Due Diligence Certificates with binding statutory undertakings signed directly by the AIF's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Compliance Officer. • For first-time fund schemes, launch permission is granted on the later of: the date of SEBI registration or 10 working days from PPM filing.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Full Form: GARUDA (Green-Channel: Alternative Investment Funds Rollout Upon Document Acknowledgement).
  • Regulatory Authority: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India).
  • Non-Accredited AIF Timeline: Cut from 30 days to 10 working days.
  • Angel & Accredited Funds: Instant green-channel fundraising; zero merchant banker certification required.
  • Undertaking Authority: Directly signed by CEO and Compliance Officer.
CAPITAL MARKETS & REGULATORY № 21

PFRDA Rolls Out Retirement Income Schemes (RIS) with Systematic Payout (SPR) and Unit Redemption (SUR)

  • Post-Retirement Pension Innovation: The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA, established under PFRDA Act, 2013; Chairman: Sivasubramanian Ramann) launched Retirement Income Schemes (RIS) under the National Pension System (NPS).
  • Addressing Superannuation Inflexibility: • Subscribers reaching 60 years previously had to mandatorily annuitize at least 40% of their accumulated corpus and withdraw the remaining 60% as a lump sum. • RIS permits retirees who do not require an immediate lump sum to remain invested in NPS up to the age of 75 or 85 years, drawing structured, tax-efficient regular income.
  • Two Flexible Post-Retirement Withdrawal Pathways:
    1. Systematic Payout Rate (SPR): • The payout rate is calibrated dynamically based on the subscriber's current age and chosen drawdown end-age. • For a subscriber exiting at age 60 and selecting an 85-year drawdown horizon, the initial annual payout begins at 4.00%, resetting annually on the subscriber's date of birth based on the prevailing net market value of the fund corpus. • Any residual corpus at the end of the drawdown horizon can be withdrawn as a lump sum or merged into an annuity.
    2. Systematic Unit Redemption (SUR): • The subscriber's total accumulated units are divided evenly across the chosen drawdown tenure. • A fixed number of mutual units are redeemed every month, providing an automated monthly cashflow irrespective of fluctuations in daily Net Asset Value (NAV).
  • NPS Regulatory Landmarks: • Open to all Indian citizens (residents, NRIs, and OCIs) aged 18 to 85 years on a voluntary basis. • Asset allocation spans 4 standardized classes: Equity (Class E), Corporate Bonds (Class C), Government Securities (Class G), and Alternative Investment Funds (Class A).
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Regulating Body: PFRDA (Chairman: Sivasubramanian Ramann; HQ: New Delhi).
  • Scheme Name: Retirement Income Schemes (RIS) under NPS.
  • Maximum Drawdown Age: Permitted up to 85 years (extended from age 75).
  • Two Withdrawal Mechanics: Systematic Payout Rate (SPR) and Systematic Unit Redemption (SUR).
  • SPR Benchmark Payout: Starts at 4% p.a. for age 60-to-85 drawdown (resets annually on birth date).
  • NPS Voluntary Entry Age: 18 to 85 years.
CAPITAL MARKETS & REGULATORY № 22

SEBI Operationalises PaRRVA Framework & Launches Mission Jagrook at 38th Foundation Day

  • Past Risk & Return Verification Agency (PaRRVA): • SEBI fully operationalized the PaRRVA Framework as India's first independent institutional verification mechanism to audit, validate, and certify past performance claims made by registered investment advisers, research analysts, and algorithmic trading platforms in advertisements. • Structure: Operates on a two-tier model comprising a Verification Body (SEBI-registered Credit Rating Agency / CRA with ≥15 years operations, ≥₹100 Cr net worth, and >250 ratings) and a PaRRVA Data Centre (PDC) operated by National Stock Exchange of India Limited (NSE) (requiring ≥₹200 Cr net worth and nationwide terminals). • Recognised CARE Ratings Limited as an accredited PaRRVA verification entity. Full commercial rollout effective May 4, 2026.
  • Mission Jagrook & 38th Foundation Day Celebrations: • Union Minister of Finance Nirmala Sitharaman delivered the keynote address at the 38th Foundation Day of SEBI (SEBI established as non-statutory body on April 12, 1988; granted statutory status under SEBI Act, 1992; Chairman: Tuhin Kanta Pandey). • Launched Mission Jagrook, a pan-India investor education and financial defense campaign to insulate retail market participants from financial influencers ('finfluencers'), fraudulent trading apps, and manipulative social media syndicates. • Introduced the SEBI Check Tool, allowing investors to independently verify bank accounts and UPI payment handles of registered market intermediaries before transferring capital. • Proposed the development of a Unified KYC System across banking, capital markets, and insurance.
  • Capital Market Milestones: • India's capital markets host over 5,900 listed companies with more than 140 million (14 crore) unique investors. • Market capitalization expanded at an annual compound rate of ~15% over the past decade; mutual fund assets grew at >20% annually; primary markets mobilize nearly ₹10 trillion (₹10 lakh crore) annually. • Central Depository Services Limited (CDSL): SEBI approved the appointment of Amit Mahajan and Nayana Ovalekar as Executive Directors on the board of CDSL.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • Performance Audit Engine: PaRRVA (Past Risk & Return Verification Agency).
  • PaRRVA Data Centre (PDC): Operated by National Stock Exchange (NSE).
  • Verification Body Partner: CARE Ratings Limited (minimum net worth ₹100 Cr).
  • Investor Defense Campaign: Mission Jagrook launched by Union Finance Minister.
  • Intermediary Payment Verifier: SEBI Check Tool.
  • Market Scale: 5,900+ listed firms, 140 million unique investors, primary markets mobilize ~₹10 Lakh Cr/year.
  • SEBI 38th Foundation Day: Established April 12, 1988 (Statutory 1992); Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey.

Rural Employment Guarantee (VB-G RAM G) Act, 2025 Enforced: 125 Days Guaranteed Work & ₹95,692 Cr Outlay

  • Historic Overhaul of Rural Employment: The Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD) notified the nationwide enforcement of the Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 [VB-G RAM G Act], effective July 1, 2026.
  • Repeal & Transition of MGNREGA: • Formally repeals the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA, 2005). • All valid e-KYC verified Job Cards issued under MGNREGA as of June 30, 2026, remain valid until transition to Gramin Rozgar Cards under the new Act.
  • Enhanced Statutory Entitlements: • Expanded Work Guarantee: Enhances the statutory employment guarantee from 100 days to 125 days of wage employment per financial year for every rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work. • Distance Allowance: If employment is provided beyond 5 km from the worker's residence, an additional 10% of the notified wage rate must be paid as a distance and transport allowance. • Delayed Compensation: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) wage payments must be processed within 3 days and reach bank/post office accounts within 15 days, failing which daily delayed compensation is legally mandated. • Worksite Childcare: For worksites with 5 or more children below five years of age, mandatory crèche facilities and an appointed woman worker caretaker paid at standard wage rates must be provided.
  • Budgetary Allocation & Funding Pattern: • Backed by the highest-ever allocation for a rural employment program: ₹95,692.31 crore for FY 2025–26 (cumulative center-state commitment expected to cross ₹1,51,000 crore). • Funding Pattern: Implemented as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) with 60:40 Centre-State cost-sharing for general states, and 90:10 for North Eastern and Himalayan states (100% for UTs without legislature).
🎯 EXAM ANGLE
  • New Rural Employment Act: VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 (repeals MGNREGA 2005).
  • Statutory Work Guarantee: 125 days per household per financial year (increased from 100 days).
  • Effective Date: July 1, 2026.
  • Distance Transport Allowance: Additional 10% wage hike for worksites >5 km.
  • Union Budget Outlay: ₹95,692.31 crore (highest-ever rural employment outlay).
  • Cost-Sharing Ratio: 60:40 (General States); 90:10 (NE & Himalayan States).

  • Direct Tax Modernisation: The Ministry of Finance (MoF / Central Board of Direct Taxes, CBDT) notified the New Income Tax Rules, 2026, replacing obsolete procedural frameworks following the passage of the Direct Tax Code reforms.
  • Strengthened Significant Economic Presence (SEP) Thresholds: • Imposes statutory corporate tax obligations on foreign digital conglomerates and cross-border SaaS/platform enterprises operating in India without a physical permanent establishment. • Revenue Threshold: Any foreign digital transaction value originating from Indian users exceeding ₹2 crore in a financial year triggers SEP taxable nexus. • User Base Threshold: Digital platforms, streaming networks, or e-commerce operators engaging with more than 3 lakh active Indian users automatically trigger SEP liability.
  • Strict 7-Year Audit Trail & Compliance Norms: • All institutional entities, corporate taxpayers, and financial intermediaries must maintain an immutable digital audit trail for a mandatory period of 7 years. • Prohibition of Tampering: Any deletion of transaction logs, modifications, or ledger alterations without a digital cryptographic trail is prohibited; monthly reporting of corrected entries is mandatory. • Strengthens corporate governance and algorithmic compliance across Indian stock exchanges and clearing houses.

MACRO • FISCAL & TAX № 2

CBDT — Income-tax Rules, 2026 & "Kar Saathi" (merged: new rules + AI assistant launch)

🪝 Hook — CBDT slimmed 511 tax rules down to 333 and rolled out an AI chatbot, "Kar Saathi," to help taxpayers navigate the new Income Tax Act, 2025 regime — effective April 1, 2026.

  • Tax Year replaces 'Previous Year'/'Assessment Year'
  • Charitable trust record: retention cut from 10 → 6 years
  • Reliefs: children's education allowance ₹100 → ₹3,000/month (max 2 children); hostel allowance → ₹9,000; employer gifts exempt up to ₹15,000; meal exemption → ₹200/meal
  • HRA exemption expanded: to Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru (50% slab, previously only 4 metros)
  • PAN mandatory for: property deals only above ₹20 lakh (up from ₹10 lakh)
  • Kar Saathi — AI-enabled 24x7 taxpayer assistant, part of 'PRARAMBH 2026' (Policy Reform and Responsible Action for Mission Viksit Bharat) campaign
  • CBDT: HQ New Delhi | Chairman Ravi Agrawal | Formed 1944

💼 Interview Q → Why replace "Previous Year/Assessment Year" with a single "Tax Year"? → Simplifies compliance under the new Income Tax Act, 2025 by removing the dual-year confusion that often causes filing errors.

🎯 EXAM ANGLE "Tax Year" terminology + PRARAMBH 2026 full form + effective date (April 1, 2026).

RBI Monetary Policy — April 2026 (FY27 First Bi-Monthly Statement)

🪝 Hook — The MPC kept rates on hold for a second straight meeting, even as it penciled in a punchy 6.9% GDP growth forecast for FY27 amid West Asia tensions.

  • Repo rate unchanged at 5.25%, stance retained "Neutral"
  • Policy Rate Corridor Structure: SDF pegged at 5.00%; MSF and Bank Rate at 5.50%; Reverse Repo at 3.35%; CRR holds at 3.00%; SLR holds at 18.00%.
  • Real GDP Growth Projections: Projected real GDP growth for FY27 at 6.9% (quarterly path: Q1 at 6.8%, Q2 at 6.7%, Q3 at 7.0%, Q4 at 7.2%).
  • Statutory Bench & Leadership: Chaired by RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra (26th Governor of RBI); 3-day bi-monthly review commenced April 6, 2026.

💼 Interview Q → Why did the RBI retain a "Neutral" stance despite steady growth? → It preserves flexibility to move rates either way as global uncertainty (West Asia tensions) clouds the outlook.

🎯 EXAM ANGLE Standing exception (always Tier A). Repo rate figure + all associated rates (SDF/MSF/CRR/SLR) are classic MCQ fodder.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 10

RBI — Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) Mandatory for Digital Payments

🪝 Hook — A single OTP will no longer cut it: from April 1, 2026, every UPI, card, and wallet transaction needs a second layer of verification.

  • Mandatory Two-Factor Scope: 2FA made compulsory across UPI, debit/credit cards, and prepaid mobile wallets — standalone SMS OTP is legally insufficient.
  • Secondary Factor Choices: Requires PIN, biometric fingerprint, hardware token, password, or facial recognition as the dynamic secondary authentication layer.
  • Institutional Liability Shift: Regulated banks and payment platforms held financially liable to compensate customers for unauthorized fraud losses arising from system vulnerabilities.
  • Staggered Compliance Timeline: Effective April 1, 2026; full enforcement across all merchant terminals and cross-border transactions mandated by October 2026.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE Effective date (Apr 1, 2026) vs full implementation date (Oct 2026) — classic date-confusion trap.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 11

RBI — Digital Payments Fraud Safeguards (Discussion Paper)

🪝 Hook — RBI's proposed fix for UPI fraud: force a one-hour "cooling-off" pause on big transfers, borrowing straight from the "golden hour" principle in crime prevention.

  • 1-hour cooling-off period proposed for A2A transfers above ₹10,000 (no chargeback option currently exists)
  • Data-Driven Fraud Threshold: Threshold chosen because ₹10,000+ transfers = ~45% of fraud cases by volume, ~98.5% by value
  • High-Value Secondary Verification: Transactions above ₹50,000 → additional verification (trusted-individual approval)
  • Mule account annual credit cap proposed at ₹25 lakh
  • New user controls: channel on/off toggle, custom limits, emergency "kill switch"

💼 Interview Q → What is the "golden hour" principle referenced by RBI? → The idea that the period immediately after a fraudulent transaction is most critical to prevent dissipation of funds — hence the proposed 1-hour delay window.

🎯 EXAM ANGLE ₹10,000 (cooling-off threshold) vs ₹50,000 (extra verification) vs ₹25 lakh (mule account cap) — three-number trap cluster.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 12

RBI — Digital Payments E-Mandate Framework, 2026

  • Registration Safeguards: Mandates initial one-time mandate registration via compulsory Additional Factor Authentication (AFA). for e-mandates
  • Pre-Debit Customer Alert: Card issuers must transmit pre-transaction debit notifications to the cardholder at least 24 hours prior to account debit.
  • Recurring transactions without: AFA up to ₹15,000; insurance/MF/credit-card bill payments without AFA up to ₹1,00,000
  • No charges may: be levied on customers for e-mandate facility
  • FASTag/NCMC auto-replenish exempted: from pre-transaction notification
🎯 EXAM ANGLE ₹15,000 (general recurring cap) vs ₹1,00,000 (insurance/MF/CC cap) is a strong trap pair.
BANKING • MONETARY POLICY № 13

RBI — NBFC Regulatory Overhaul Cluster (merged: 3-layer proposal, NBFC-UL threshold change, branch authorisation, TReDS)

🪝 Hook — RBI is rewriting the NBFC rulebook on three fronts at once: how NBFCs are layered, how the "upper layer" is defined, and how easily they can open branches.

  • A. Proposed new 3-layer framework (Upper/Middle/Lower) to replace existing 4-layer Scale-Based Regulation (Base/Middle/Upper/Top, Oct 2021)
  • B. Proposed replacing NBFC-UL identification methodology with a flat ₹1 lakh crore asset threshold (vs. current Top-10 + parametric scoring: 70% quantitative, 30% qualitative); to be reviewed every 5 years. Also proposed removing the carve-out that shielded govt-owned NBFCs (NABARD, Exim Bank, SIDBI) from UL classification — aligning to "ownership-neutral regulation"
  • C. NBFC Branch Authorisation, 2026 — NBFCs can open branches without prior RBI approval based on Net Owned Funds (NOF) & credit rating thresholds (₹50 crore NOF / AA rating benchmark)
  • D. Proposed dropping due-diligence requirement for MSMEs onboarding TReDS (Trade Receivables Discounting System)

⏰ Status flag → All four are draft/proposed as of April 2026 — check for finalisation before exam.

🎯 EXAM ANGLE ₹1 lakh crore NBFC-UL threshold is the standout figure across this cluster.

DISPATCH № 26

India's 100 GW Nuclear Power Roadmap by 2047

🪝 Hook — India wants to go from 8.8 GW to 100 GW of nuclear power in 21 years — but first it needs to cut approval timelines almost in half.

  • Long-Term Nuclear Target: Ambition to expand nuclear power capacity to 100 GW by 2047 from the baseline of 8.8 GW (an over 10-fold expansion).
  • Enabling Statutory Framework: Anchored by the proposed SHANTI Act (Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India).
  • Regulatory Clearance Compression: Slashes statutory nuclear project approval cycles from 13 years down to 8–9 years.
  • Capital Investment Requirement: Total required capital investment estimated at ≥₹20 lakh crore based on an industry baseline of ₹22 crore per MW.

MACRO • FISCAL & TAX № 1

India's Economy — Size, Growth & the Feb 1 Budget (merged: Jan's pre-Budget context + Feb's actual Budget content)

🪝 Hook — India overtook Japan to become the world's 4th-largest economy in January, and a month later Nirmala Sitharaman used her record 9th-consecutive Budget to lock in a falling fiscal deficit and a ₹1,000 crore semiconductor push.

  • Global Economic Milestone: India officially surpassed Japan to become the **world's 4th-largest economy with a GDP of 4.18trillion∗∗,targeting3rdpositionby2030byovertakingGermany(4.18 trillion**, targeting 3rd position by 2030 by overtaking Germany (4.18trillion∗∗,targeting3rdpositionby2030byovertakingGermany(7.3 trillion projected).
  • Quarterly & Annual GDP Trajectory: Real GDP expanded by 8.2% in Q2 FY26 (accelerating from 7.8% in Q1 and 7.4% in Q4 FY25); the National Statistical Office (NSO) 1st Advance Estimates pegged FY26 real GDP growth at 7.4% (₹201.90 lakh crore).
  • Economic Survey 2025-26 Projections: Tabled on January 29 by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and authored by CEA V. Anantha Nageswaran; projected FY27 real GDP growth at 6.8%–7.2%; banking health strengthened with Gross NPA at 2.2% and Net NPA at 0.5% (Sep 2025); fiscal deficit projected to decline to 4.4% of GDP in FY26 (down from 9.2% in FY21).
  • Global Agency Forecast Consensus: Multilateral institutions aligned around moderated growth — World Bank projected 6.5%, IMF forecast 6.6%/6.2%, and Moody's projected 6.4%/6.5% (OECD, S&P, ADB, and Fitch projected within a similar 6.3%–6.7% band).
  • Union Budget 2026-27 Record Presentation: Presented on February 1, 2026, marking Nirmala Sitharaman's 9th consecutive Union Budget, setting a new all-time record for consecutive presentations (Morarji Desai retains the record for most Budgets overall at 10, non-consecutive).
  • Institutional & Thematic Blueprint: First Budget prepared in the newly commissioned Kartavya Bhawan; anchored around three core 'Kartavyas' — accelerating economic growth, fulfilling citizen aspirations, and building inclusive development.
  • Fiscal Consolidation & Debt Metrics: Fiscal deficit for FY27 targeted down to 4.3% of GDP (from 4.4% Revised Estimate in FY26); Central Government Debt-to-GDP ratio projected at 55.6% (BE 2026-27) versus 56.1% (RE 2025-26); Capital Expenditure (Capex) hiked 9% to a historic high of ₹12.2 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP).
  • Direct Tax Code Modernisation: Enacted the New Income Tax Act, 2025, effective April 1, 2026, drastically slashing total sections from 819 down to 536 to simplify compliance.
  • Financial Market & Capital Taxation: Securities Transaction Tax (STT) increased on Futures to 0.05% (from 0.02%) and on Options to 0.15%; share buyback taxation revised to 22% for corporate promoters and 30% for non-corporate promoters.
  • Strategic Industrial & Infrastructure Outlays: Launched India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) 2.0 with a ₹1,000 crore FY27 outlay; announced 'Biopharma SHAKTI' (₹10,000 crore), the SME Growth Fund (₹10,000 crore), and 7 new High-Speed Rail corridors (₹16 lakh crore).
  • 16th Finance Commission Devolution: Accepted recommendations of the Commission (chaired by Dr. Arvind Panagariya); retained vertical tax devolution to states at 41% (for 2026-27 to 2030-31); introduced a new 10% weightage for 'Contribution to GDP' (replacing the 2.5% weightage for 'Tax & Fiscal Effort'); total grants to states fixed at ₹9.47 lakh crore.
  • Gender Budgeting Expansion: Gender Budget Statement (GBS) share rose to 9.37% of total budget expenditure (up from 8.86%), with total allocation reaching ₹5.01 lakh crore (+11.55% YoY).

🧠 Mnemonic → "9th, 4.3, 4.4" — 9th consecutive Budget, 4.3% fiscal deficit target, 4.4% capex-to-GDP.

MACRO • FISCAL & TAX № 2

India's Fiscal Deficit Tracking — interim data (Apr-Nov & Apr-Dec 2025)

  • 8-Month Fiscal Deficit (Apr–Nov 2025): India's fiscal deficit reached ₹9.76 lakh crore, representing 62.3% of the full-year Budget Estimate (widened from 52.5% during the corresponding period last year), supported by an RBI dividend transfer to the Centre of ₹2.69 lakh crore.
  • 9-Month Fiscal Turnaround (Apr–Dec 2025): The cumulative deficit narrowed sharply to ₹8.55 lakh crore, or 54.5% of the annual estimate, aided by an extraordinary December fiscal surplus of ₹1.21 trillion generated through quarterly corporate advance-tax inflows.
  • Reconciliation with Annual Budget: This interim high-frequency tracking preceded the Union Budget's FY26 Revised Estimate of 4.4% of GDP, demonstrating how mid-year fiscal compression stabilized the annual fiscal deficit path.
🎯 EXAM ANGLE Don't confuse the 8-month (62.3%) and 9-month (54.5%) figures; note how the rare December surplus (₹1.21T) narrowed the cumulative deficit by nearly 8 percentage points.

Startup India — Redefinition to Include Deep Tech (Feb)

  • Regulatory Framework Modernisation: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) amended startup recognition norms, establishing distinct statutory criteria for conventional vs deep-technology ventures.
  • Standard Startup Eligibility Limits: A business entity is recognized as a standard startup for up to 10 years from the date of incorporation, provided annual turnover does not exceed ₹200 crore.
  • Deep Tech Startup Extended Thresholds: To accommodate longer gestation and research timelines, deep-tech startups receive an extended eligibility window of 20 years and an increased turnover ceiling of ₹300 crore.
  • Ecosystem Scale & Institutional Support: India crossed 200,000+ officially recognized startups since the 2016 launch, financed through dedicated instruments: Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS), Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups (CGSS), and SIPP.
